article_title: Automating Learner Assessment: Benchmarking Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for EEG-Based Familiarity Prediction
citation: Isuru Nanayakkara and Thilina Halloluwa. (2026). Automating Learner Assessment: Benchmarking Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for EEG-Based Familiarity Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16541
title: EEG familiarity benchmark dataset and evaluation framework (3960 samples, 23 participants, two validation protocols)
description: The article releases the description of a benchmarking framework for EEG-based familiarity prediction: continuous EEG from 23 participants viewing familiar and unfamiliar faces and mathematical equations, preprocessed in EEGLAB and reduced to 84 Power Spectral Density features (14 channels × 6 bands), yielding "a feature vector of 84 features (14 channels×6 bands) per epoch" and a final dataset of 3960 samples. It pairs the dataset with two validation protocols — leaky Stratified K-Fold and trial-independent Group K-Fold — to expose temporal leakage, plus LOGO domain-separated evaluations and permutation significance testing.
requirements: Familiarity ground truth established via a pre-experiment questionnaire in which participants confirmed recognition of each stimulus
Class-balanced weights and weighted F1 to handle the imbalance between stimulus domains (Equations: 2559 samples, Faces: 1401 samples)
constraints: Participant identifiers were not retained, so strict subject-level Group K-Fold cannot be guaranteed and cross-subject leakage remains possible
Manual ICA selection and artifact rejection introduce subjectivity
4 Hz frequency resolution makes narrow bands like Delta difficult to isolate
target_learners: adult volunteers aged 20-30 with science and mathematics backgrounds
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of familiarity with factual knowledge (faces) and conceptual knowledge (mathematical equations)
examples: Participants silently counted familiar items in each block of 40 familiar and 40 unfamiliar images, each displayed for 2.5 seconds with a 1.5-second interstimulus interval
key_sources: Isuru Nanayakkara and Thilina Halloluwa. (2026). Automating Learner Assessment: Benchmarking Machine Learning and Deep Learning Models for EEG-Based Familiarity Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16541

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: EEG-fNIRS bimodal complementarity framework for attention quantification
description: The article's attention modeling framework rests on the complementary strengths of EEG and fNIRS. EEG offers millisecond-level temporal resolution sensitive to rapid stimulus changes but is susceptible to motion artifacts, while fNIRS suffers hemodynamic latency yet provides region-level spatial specificity and greater tolerance to movement. As the authors state, "EEG primarily contributes high-temporal-resolution neural dynamics, whereas fNIRS provides complementary region-level spatial information over the targeted cortical regions." These complementary properties motivate the bimodal input, with fused features feeding a DDQN that outputs high, medium, or low attention levels.
requirements: Simultaneous EEG and fNIRS acquisition over prefrontal and temporal regions subserving attention and audiovisual cognitive processing
constraints: The channel layout can only bias measured data toward top-down control and multimodal integration and cannot completely separate them
target_learners: pilot-cohort students watching instructional videos in video-based learning
target_learning_goals: stable, accurate, temporally fine-grained quantification of student attention during instructional video viewing
examples: Channels were placed over prefrontal and temporal regions, deliberately avoiding the occipital lobe to prevent early visual responses from contaminating recordings
key_sources: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Educational escape rooms as an instructional concept grounded in game methods adapted to learning goals
description: An educational escape room transfers the methods of a commercial escape room - "live action team-based games where players discover clues, solve puzzles, and accomplish tasks" (quoting Nicholson's definition) - to a learning context with a defined learning goal tailored to a target group. Puzzles and challenges align with curriculum content, often through a background story, creating authentic learning contexts that encourage meaningful activity and provide space for failure. Variants include pop-up rooms, puzzle boxes, puzzle hunts, serial stories, hybrid games, and virtual EERs. The review describes EERs as implemented in primary/secondary education, higher education, and professional development.
requirements: A defined learning goal tailored to a specific target group must be prioritized over the game mechanics alone
Time limits typically adjusted to fit within school hours or teaching units
constraints: The review restricts its analysis to formal educational settings and articles developed by lecturers rather than students
examples: Bassford et al.'s 'CrashEd' embeds STEM subjects into a realistic criminal case
Around 79% of EERs are utilized in classrooms or laboratories, per Fotaris and Mastoras (2019)
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Six patterns of theoretical integration in EER research, from general statements to empirical validation
description: The review develops a six-category typology of how deeply EER articles integrate theory, classifying each of the 24 included articles along four dimensions: didactic considerations, implementation of a specific EER, theoretical foundation connected with didactic considerations, and empirical verification of the theoretical foundation. The patterns range from "general statements on theoretical grounding in EERs without connection to didactic considerations" through loose connections, combined theoretical-didactic treatments without a specific EER or without empirical validation, up to "theoretical grounding with empirical validation". Each pattern is labeled with the dominant category of its articles.
requirements: Articles must be classifiable on the four dimensions of didactic considerations, specific EER implementation, theory-didactics connection, and empirical verification
constraints: The typology was developed from only 24 articles that passed a strict theoretical-foundation screening criterion
target_learning_goals: understanding the theoretical integration of instructional design in EERs
examples: Abdul Rahim et al. (2022) exemplifies general statements without didactic connection, where SDT classification appeared only in the discussion without relating findings to it
Piñero (2020) exemplifies combining theoretical grounding and didactic considerations without empirical validation
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review
citation: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625
title: Debriefing as the structured consolidation phase of experiential learning in EERs
description: Within experiential learning in EERs, a sequenced debriefing phase operationalizes reflective observation and abstract conceptualization, and was "extensively discussed in seven articles" of the review. The emphasis lies in self-assessment and critical reflection on performance, re-expressing learning objectives, discussing emotions and approaches during the game, and providing feedback on cooperation and to game developers. Implementations may start with an outro video, prepared questions on learning objectives and team-based skills, and open-ended questions to initiate dialogue; Fotaris and Mastoras (2022) suggested the reflection phase take up approximately one-third of lesson time.
requirements: Learning objectives must be clearly expressed once again during debriefing
Reflection should be planned as a substantial share of lesson time (about one-third suggested)
constraints: Debriefing descriptions come from development/evaluation articles; the review reports no effect sizes for debriefing
examples: Egan et al. (2021) mapped Kolb's four abilities of effective learners onto their EER, with sequenced debrief covering reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation
key_sources: Vorderobermeier, A., Abel, J., & Sailer, M. (2024). Theoretical foundations and approaches in research on educational escape rooms: A systematic review. Educational Research Review, 44, 100625. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100625

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement
citation: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4
title: Electroencephalography (EEG) as a continuous, objective, online measure of cognitive load
description: Antonenko et al. (2010) describe the possibilities offered by "electroencephalography (EEG) to provide a continuous and objective measure of cognitive load". Unlike offline mental-effort ratings, online process measures indicate cognitive load at specific points in time, allowing hypotheses to be tested in more detail. The element identifies which EEG components can assess load and reviews EEG studies of learning from hypertext and multimedia materials.
requirements: Rapid technological advances making online, continuous measurement methods accessible to educational researchers
constraints: Offline measures such as mental effort ratings yield only indirect evidence because they do not capture load at the relevant specific points in time
target_learners: participants learning from hypertext and multimedia materials
target_learning_goals: measuring cognitive load during learning from multimedia and hypertext
examples: Antonenko and Niederhauser (2010) used EEG's fine temporal resolution to detect load differences when participants accessed hyperlinks with or without content-preview leads
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4

article_title: Supplemental Material for Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests
citation: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp
title: EEG-alpha task-related synchronization as an inferred measure of internal attention
description: The article frames alpha rhythms (8-13 Hz) as sensory gating rather than cortical idling: alpha synchronization suppresses responsiveness of networks to irrelevant sensory input, allowing priority processing of internal processes such as top-down predictions. Internal attention is inferred from alpha task-related synchronization computed against a person-specific baseline, using a person-specific peak alpha frequency identified via Klimesch's lowest-desynchronization criterion.
requirements: A non-task baseline recording is required to compute task-related synchronization relative to each person's own baseline
constraints: The study's equipment had insufficient electrodes for spatial localization, so spatial information was excluded
target_learning_goals: inferring students' internal attentional focus during science tasks and tests
examples: High alpha task-related synchronization indicates a focus on internal processes, while low synchronization indicates focus on external stimuli
key_sources: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp

article_title: Supplemental Material for Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests
citation: Kennett, R., Martin, A. J., Pearson, J., Burns, E. C., & Collie, R. (2025). Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000964.supp
title: EEG-theta task-related synchronization as an exploratory inferred measure of working memory activity
description: The article links theta oscillations to encoding of new information via hippocampo-cortical feedback loops, with higher theta power indicating more efficient memory circuits and greater access to working memory. EEG-theta is computed as the proportionalized difference between task and baseline theta power over a person-specific band defined 6 to 4 Hz below the individual's peak alpha frequency, used exploratively alongside other indicators.
requirements: Theta power must be referenced to an individual's own baseline and proportionalized to account for factors such as scalp thickness and electrode connection
constraints: The article cautions that theta synchronization is linked to working memory but is not its sole determinant, necessitating cautious interpretation
target_learning_goals: inferring working memory activity during classroom science assessment
examples: Castro-Meneses et al. (2019) identified a correlation between theta power and cognitive load, suggesting theta as a real-time measure of working memory activity

article_title: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity
citation: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity. (2024). npj Science of Learning 9, 27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00240-y
title: Modified and emerging EEG hardware for dense, curly, and styled hair, including caps with elongated pedestals and dry comb electrodes
description: The review describes hardware accommodations for hair diversity: Magstim EGI “now allows for ordering caps with elongated pedestals, which allow for more space for hair between the cap and scalp,” and dry comb electrodes entering the market penetrate hair — including long-lasting styles like braids and locs — without post-visit washing. Etienne and colleagues designed a novel electrode for reliable EEG recordings on coarse and curly hair, and analytical efforts are underway to account for hair texture and volume differences.
requirements: Novel electrodes are not currently available for most pediatric EEG systems and require a specific braiding pattern.
constraints: The review notes it is unclear how specialized electrodes, increased pedestal lengths, and increased scalp oils from not pre-washing hair may impact the EEG signal.
target_learners: Infants and young children with dense, curly, or styled hair participating in EEG research
target_learning_goals: Enabling high-quality EEG data collection across hair types so developmental findings generalize across racial and ethnic groups
examples: Figure 2 of the review compares a cap modified with elongated sponges and pedestals to a typical cap with shorter sponges and pedestals.
key_sources: Fostering inclusion in EEG measures of pediatric brain activity. (2024). npj Science of Learning 9, 27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00240-y

article_title: Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors
citation: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6
title: EER-Tutor: a Web-enabled constraint-based tutor for Enhanced Entity Relationship modeling
description: EER-Tutor is a Web-enabled re-implementation of KERMIT, developed in the WETAS authoring shell, supporting the Enhanced Entity Relationship model with specializations and categories. Its interface shows requirements at the top, an EER toolbar, a drawing area where incorrect parts are highlighted in red, and a feedback pane. It is one of three tutors available on Addison-Wesley's DatabasePlace portal, "used by more than 10,000 students worldwide", and its code was the foundation for COLLECT-UML and research on metacognitive skills, affect-sensitive agents, and tutorial dialogues.
requirements: Developed in WETAS, the authoring shell for constraint-based ITSs
constraints: The current version contains 57 problems and over 200 constraints
target_learners: students learning database design worldwide via the DatabasePlace portal
target_learning_goals: Enhanced Entity Relationship modeling and database design
examples: An affect-sensitive agent tracked students' facial features and problem-solving actions and responded with affect-sensitive feedback such as encouraging a struggling student to try simpler problems
key_sources: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6

article_title: Review of EEF Projects. Evaluation Report
citation: Demack, S., Maxwell, B., Coldwell, M., Stevens, A., Wolstenholme, C., Reaney-Wood, S., Stiell, B., & Lortie-Forgues, H. (2021). Review of EEF projects: Evaluation report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Five-theme theoretical framework for grouping explanatory variables in meta-analyses of intervention trial effect sizes
description: The review developed a theoretical framework derived from literature with "five overarching themes to group explanatory variables": Intervention, Implementation & fidelity, Theory & evidence, Context, and Evaluation design. Each theme contains coded explanatory variables (e.g. curriculum focus, cost, CPD provision, trial design) used to structure subgroup meta-analyses of the effect sizes reported by the 82 EEF trials. The framework was developed focusing on primary ITT outcomes and adapted for secondary and FSM analyses.
requirements: Explanatory variables must be coded at evaluation level from trial reports for each theme before subgroup meta-analyses can be run
constraints: Psychological outcomes were excluded from the framework-based meta-analyses because of their distinct and diverse nature
target_learners: primary and secondary school pupils in England, including FSM pupils
target_learning_goals: attainment outcomes in curriculum areas such as English and maths
examples: The review coded variables such as curriculum area, intervention cost, direct implementer, CPD provision and trial design under the five themes and ran subgroup meta-analyses for each
key_sources: Demack, S., Maxwell, B., Coldwell, M., Stevens, A., Wolstenholme, C., Reaney-Wood, S., Stiell, B., & Lortie-Forgues, H. (2021). Review of EEF projects: Evaluation report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625480

article_title: Improving 7th Grade Students' Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model
citation: Kızkapan, O., & Bektaş, O. (2021). Improving 7th Grade Students’ Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model. Pedagogical Research, 6(3), em0095. https://doi.org/10.29333/pr/10949
title: Epistemologically Enriched Toulmin Argumentation Model (EETAM)
description: EETAM is a modified version of Toulmin's argumentation model in which, after students build a first argument (A0) about subject knowledge through TAM, the teacher opens a second argumentation round (A1) on a dimension of epistemological beliefs. The article states that "The argument developed in the first stage (A0) serves as data, warrant, backing or rebuttal in the new argument on epistemological beliefs (A1)", so subject-matter learning feeds explicit epistemological discussion. It was implemented over six weeks in a 7th-grade structure and properties of matter unit, covering Schommer's dimensions week by week.
requirements: Students first learn the science topic through Toulmin argumentation so that a first argument (A0) exists to be reused in the epistemological argument (A1)
A teacher trained to initiate and lead explicit discussions on epistemological belief dimensions
constraints: Tested only in 7th-grade science (structure and properties of matter) over six weeks in one Turkish public school
target_learning_goals: Epistemological beliefs about the certainty, source and development of scientific knowledge
Structure and properties of matter subject knowledge
examples: In week two, students discussed which atomic model is accepted today (A0), then EETAM students began a second discussion on the certainty and empirical nature of scientific knowledge using what they had learned (A1)
key_sources: Kızkapan, O., & Bektaş, O. (2021). Improving 7th Grade Students’ Epistemological Beliefs by Epistemologically Enriched Argumentation Model. Pedagogical Research, 6(3), em0095. https://doi.org/10.29333/pr/10949

article_title: What do physiotherapists find useful in e-learning interventions to improve their knowledge, attitudes and beliefs on low back pain management: a nested qualitative study from an educational randomized clinical trial.
citation: Vanderstraeten Rob, Fourré Antoine, Demoulin Christophe, Michielsen Jozef, Bastiaens Hilde, Roussel Nathalie, Anthierens Sibyl. (2025). What do physiotherapists find useful in e-learning interventions to improve their knowledge, attitudes and beliefs on low back pain management: a nested qualitative study from an educational randomized clinical trial. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-025-03032-4
title: Experimental vs traditional e-learning interventions for physiotherapists' low back pain management
description: Two three-module (30 min each) e-learning interventions, both based on the same LBP clinical guidelines, were compared in the RCT. The EEI "contained interactive modules with the inclusion of menus, videos, simulated clinical situations, metaphors, voice-overs and quizzes", let participants control their pace, and demonstrated guideline application pragmatically; the TEI was lecture-based, theoretical, without interaction or clinical examples, and pace-controlled only by watching and pausing. This nested qualitative study evaluated participants' experiences of both interventions' content.
requirements: Developed by a multidisciplinary expert team of academics and clinicians and based on recent LBP clinical guidelines and a prior pilot study
constraints: The TEI provided no interaction or clinical examples and did not allow pace control beyond watching and pausing
target_learners: Licensed physiotherapists in Belgium and France actively managing patients with low back pain
target_learning_goals: Improving knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs toward a biopsychosocial, guideline-consistent approach to LBP management
examples: EEI module 3 explained and reassured patients about the pain experience using videos, metaphors, and infographics; TEI module 3 covered neurophysiology of pain theory and pain definitions
key_sources: Vanderstraeten Rob, Fourré Antoine, Demoulin Christophe, Michielsen Jozef, Bastiaens Hilde, Roussel Nathalie, Anthierens Sibyl. (2025). What do physiotherapists find useful in e-learning interventions to improve their knowledge, attitudes and beliefs on low back pain management: a nested qualitative study from an educational randomized clinical trial. BMC Primary Care. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-025-03032-4

article_title: Undergraduate e-learning programmes in health professions: An integrative review of evaluation standards in low- and middle-income countries.
citation: Mutua Moses M., Nyoni Champion N. (2023). Undergraduate e-learning programmes in health professions: An integrative review of evaluation standards in low- and middle-income countries. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281586
title: E-learning Educational Atmosphere Measure (EEAM), a 40-item instrument covering six factors of the e-learning educational environment
description: EEAM is an instrument developed by Mousavi et al. (2020), one of the eight studies included in the review, for assessing e-students' perception of the educational environment. An expert committee drafted 43 items, reviewed by further experts for face validity, and administered to 185 students studying virtual programmes. The review reports that "The final instrument, named as 'e-learning Educational Atmosphere Measure' (EEAM), included 40 questions that covered six factors consisting of programme effectiveness, teaching quality, ethics and professionalism, learner support, safety and convenience, and awareness of the rules."
requirements: Suitable for interactive e-learning courses applying a wide range of synchronous and asynchronous strategies
constraints: Designed for current interactive e-learning courses, per the review's report of the source study
target_learners: students studying virtual programmes in e-learning settings
target_learning_goals: assessing students' perception of the e-learning educational atmosphere to improve e-classes and learning outcomes
examples: The instrument was presented to 185 students studying virtual programmes by e-mail or in-person, using 5-point Likert-scale items
key_sources: Mutua Moses M., Nyoni Champion N. (2023). Undergraduate e-learning programmes in health professions: An integrative review of evaluation standards in low- and middle-income countries. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0281586
